docs.title: crawl_github_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_github_files(repo_url: str, token: str | None = None, max_file_size: int = 1 * 1024 * 1024, use_relative_paths: bool = False, include_patterns: str | set[str] | None = None, exclude_patterns: str | set[str] | None = None) -> dict:

Description: Crawls and ingests source files from a remote GitHub repository. If the repo_url points to an SSH Git endpoint (starting with git@ or ending with .git), it clones the target repository into a temporary directory, filters the filesystem against .gitignore and pattern criteria, and returns the file contents. For HTTP/HTTPS GitHub URLs, it parses the repository coordinates, resolves refs (branches or tree SHAs) against the GitHub REST API, and recursively traverses the contents tree.

During execution, it manages GitHub API rate limits by reading the X-RateLimit-Reset header and pausing execution when rate limits are reached. It rejects non-text/binary files, enforces byte size limits (max_file_size), and supports re-rooting dictionary keys to relative subdirectories.

Parameters: * repo_url (str): URL of the GitHub repository. Supports SSH clone URLs (e.g., git@github.com:...) or deep HTTPS tree URLs (e.g., 'https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/e45a15766746d95f8cfaaa705b0371267bec812e/python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core'). * token (str | None, optional): GitHub personal access token used in the Authorization: token <token> header. Required for private repositories and recommended for public repos to prevent rate limiting. Defaults to None. * max_file_size (int, optional): Maximum allowed size in bytes per file before exclusion. Defaults to 1048576 (1 MB). * use_relative_paths (bool, optional): When True, returned dictionary keys are stripped of the base directory path prefix. Defaults to False. * include_patterns (str | set[str] | None, optional): Wildcard pattern or set of patterns (e.g., "*.py", {"*.md", "*.txt"}) matched against filenames using fnmatch. If None, all files are accepted. Defaults to None. * exclude_patterns (str | set[str] | None, optional): Wildcard pattern or set of patterns matched against file paths to exclude files or directories. Defaults to None.

Returns: * dict: Dictionary containing two top-level keys: * "files" (dict[str, str]): Mapping of file paths to their UTF-8 string contents. * "stats" (dict[str, Any]): Execution statistics including downloaded_count, skipped_count, skipped_files, base_path, include_patterns, and exclude_patterns.

Raises: * ValueError: Raised when an HTTPS GitHub URL does not contain at least owner and repo path parts. * Exception: Raised when GitHub API rate limits (HTTP status 403 or 429) are encountered and no token is provided.

def crawl_github_files(
    repo_url,
    token=None,
    max_file_size: int = 1 * 1024 * 1024,  # 1 MB
    use_relative_paths: bool = False,
    include_patterns: str | set[str] | None = None,
    exclude_patterns: str | set[str] | None = None,
):
    # Convert single pattern to set
    if include_patterns and isinstance(include_patterns, str):
        include_patterns = {include_patterns}
    if exclude_patterns and isinstance(exclude_patterns, str):
        exclude_patterns = {exclude_patterns}

    # ... [Internal helper definitions and branching logic] ...

    # Detect SSH URL (git@ or .git suffix)
    is_ssh_url = repo_url.startswith("git@") or repo_url.endswith(".git")

    if is_ssh_url:
        # Clone repo via SSH to temp dir
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdirname:
            print(f"Cloning SSH repo {repo_url} to temp dir {tmpdirname} ...")
            try:
                repo = git.Repo.clone_from(repo_url, tmpdirname)
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error cloning repo: {e}")
                return {"files": {}, "stats": {"error": str(e)}}

            # ... [Walk temp directory and process files] ...

    # ... [REST API URL parsing, ref resolution, and recursive crawl] ...

The function normalizes pattern parameters by converting singular strings into set collections. When handling SSH endpoints, it delegates the clone operation to git.Repo.clone_from using a context-managed tempfile.TemporaryDirectory. When handling standard GitHub web URLs, it extracts path tokens to resolve repository coordinates before beginning API traversal.

Example: 

github_token = os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN")
repo_url = "https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/tree/6c38dc93f40a47f4d1350adca9ec0d72502e223f/pydantic"

result = crawl_github_files(
    repo_url,
    token=github_token,
    max_file_size=1 * 1024 * 1024,
    use_relative_paths=True,
    include_patterns={"*.py", "*.md"},
)

files = result["files"]
stats = result["stats"]

docs.title: should_include_file()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Internal Closure Helper) Signature: def should_include_file(file_path: str, file_name: str, gitignore_spec: pathspec.PathSpec | None = None) -> bool:

Description: Evaluates whether a candidate file matches the active inclusion rules, is not matched by repository .gitignore specifications, and does not match explicit exclusion wildcards.

Parameters: * file_path (str): The relative or repository path of the candidate file. * file_name (str): The base filename (e.g., main.py). * gitignore_spec (pathspec.PathSpec | None, optional): Compiled pathspec matcher containing .gitignore patterns. Defaults to None.

Returns: * bool: True if the file satisfies all inclusion/exclusion rules; False if it should be skipped.

    def should_include_file(file_path: str, file_name: str, gitignore_spec=None) -> bool:
        """Determine if a file should be included based on patterns"""
        # If no include patterns are specified, include all files
        if not include_patterns:
            include_file = True
        else:
            # Check if file matches any include pattern
            include_file = any(fnmatch.fnmatch(file_name, pattern) for pattern in include_patterns)

        # Check gitignore if provided
        if include_file and gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(file_path):
            return False

        # If exclude patterns are specified, check if file should be excluded
        if exclude_patterns and include_file:
            # Exclude if file matches any exclude pattern
            exclude_file = any(fnmatch.fnmatch(file_path, pattern) for pattern in exclude_patterns)
            return not exclude_file

        return include_file

The filter evaluates criteria in three sequential stages. First, if include_patterns is defined, the base file_name is evaluated using fnmatch.fnmatch. Second, if a gitignore_spec is provided, file_path is evaluated against it, immediately returning False on a match. Third, if exclude_patterns are present, the full file_path is checked against each pattern, excluding matching files.

docs.title: fetch_branches()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Internal Closure Helper) Signature: def fetch_branches(owner: str, repo: str) -> list[dict]:

Description: Queries the GitHub API endpoint /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches to list all branches in the target repository. Used to determine whether a segment in the URL represents a branch name.

Parameters: * owner (str): The repository owner or organization account. * repo (str): The repository name.

Returns: * list[dict]: List of branch dictionaries returned by the GitHub API. Returns an empty list [] on HTTP 404 or other non-200 responses.

Raises: * Exception: Raised if HTTP status 403 or 429 is received and no token was configured.

    def fetch_branches(owner: str, repo: str):
        """Get brancshes of the repository"""

        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches"
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and not token:
            raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")

        if response.status_code == 404:
            if not token:
                print(
                    "Error 404: Repository not found or is private.\n"
                    "If this is a private repository, please provide a valid GitHub token via the 'token' argument or set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable."
                )
            else:
                print(
                    "Error 404: Repository not found or insufficient permissions with the provided token.\n"
                    "Please verify the repository exists and the token has access to this repository."
                )
            return []

        if response.status_code != 200:
            print(f"Error fetching the branches of {owner}/{repo}: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
            return []

        return response.json()

The function executes a requests.get with a 30-second connection and read timeout. It inspects status codes to distinguish between authentication errors, repository absence, and rate-limit exhaustion.

Description: Validates whether a specific Git tree or commit SHA exists in the remote GitHub repository by issuing a GET request to /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{tree}.

    def check_tree(owner: str, repo: str, tree: str):
        """Check the repository has the given tree"""

        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{tree}"
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and not token:

        return response.status_code == 200

This function performs a low-overhead ref validation check when a path segment in a GitHub /tree/... URL does not match any known branch name, verifying whether the identifier is a commit or tree SHA.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils.crawl_local_files module implements a filesystem crawler designed to traverse local directory trees, parse file contents, and collect text data into an in-memory dictionary. It serves as the local counterpart to crawl_github_files, sharing a standardized return schema ({"files": {filepath: content}}) to provide pipeline nodes with an agnostic ingestion interface.

The crawler performs a single-pass traversal using os.walk, dynamically pruning directories in place to prevent unnecessary filesystem traversal. It applies a multi-tiered filtering pipeline in the following sequence:

  1. Gitignore Evaluation: Parses root .gitignore files using pathspec with gitwildmatch rules.
  2. Directory Exclusion Filtering: Evaluates directory paths against caller-specified glob exclusion rules and prunes matched directories from os.walk traversal.
  3. File Exclusion Filtering: Checks files against user-defined exclusion patterns using fnmatch.
  4. File Inclusion Filtering: Validates files against inclusion rules (when specified).
  5. Size Limit Checking: Rejects files exceeding byte-threshold constraints using os.path.getsize.
  6. UTF-8 Ingestion and Decoding: Attempts decoding using utf-8-sig to handle byte order marks (BOM) gracefully while filtering out non-text/binary files.

The module provides colored terminal diagnostics using ANSI escape codes and generates an execution summary detailing processed files, exclusions, size rejections, and binary decode failures.

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_local_files(directory, include_patterns=None, exclude_patterns=None, max_file_size=None, use_relative_paths=True) -> dict

Description: Crawls a local directory tree recursively, applying exclusion rules, .gitignore wildcards, inclusion patterns, size thresholds, and text encoding checks. Extracted file contents are returned in a dictionary keyed by file path.

Parameters: * directory (str): The path to the root directory on the local filesystem to crawl. * include_patterns (set, optional): Glob patterns defining which files to include (e.g., {"*.py", "*.js"}). Defaults to None. * exclude_patterns (set, optional): Glob patterns defining files or directories to exclude (e.g., {"tests/*", "*.pyc"}). Defaults to None. * max_file_size (int, optional): The maximum allowable file size in bytes. Files exceeding this threshold are skipped. Defaults to None. * use_relative_paths (bool, optional): When True, returned dictionary keys are formatted relative to directory. When False, keys contain the full path. Defaults to True.

Returns: * dict: A dictionary containing a single key "files", mapping string file paths to their decoded string contents: {"files": {filepath: content}}.

Raises: * ValueError: Raised if directory does not exist or is not a valid filesystem directory.

def crawl_local_files(
    directory,
    include_patterns=None,
    exclude_patterns=None,
    max_file_size=None,
    use_relative_paths=True,
):
    if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- ANSI colors ---
    C_GREEN = "\033[92m"
    C_GRAY = "\033[90m"
    C_RED = "\033[91m"
    C_RESET = "\033[0m"

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []

    # --- Load .gitignore ---
    gitignore_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    gitignore_spec = None
    if os.path.exists(gitignore_path):
        try:
            with open(gitignore_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                gitignore_patterns = f.readlines()
            gitignore_spec = pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", gitignore_patterns)
            print(f"Loaded .gitignore patterns from {gitignore_path}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Warning: Could not read or parse .gitignore file {gitignore_path}: {e}")

    # ... (directory walking and file filtering logic) ...

The initialization block validates the existence of the target root path via os.path.isdir, raising a ValueError immediately if invalid. It initializes tracking counters for CLI reporting and attempts to discover a .gitignore file located directly within directory. When present, lines are read using utf-8-sig encoding and compiled into a pathspec.PathSpec object using the standard gitwildmatch syntax. If .gitignore reading fails, the error is caught and reported to standard output without interrupting the crawl.

    # --- Single-pass: walk, filter, and process inline ---
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        # --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, d), directory)

            reason = None
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(dirpath_rel):
                reason = "excluded (.gitignore)"
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern.removesuffix("/*")
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = "excluded"
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {dirpath_rel}/ [{reason}]{C_RESET}")

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()

        # ... (file filtering and ingestion logic) ...

Directory pruning is performed inside the os.walk loop before recursing into subdirectories. Each directory name in dirs is converted to a relative path and checked against the compiled gitignore_spec and the caller's exclude_patterns. Patterns suffixed with /* are normalized using removesuffix("/*") to ensure matching on directory names and paths. Directories identified for exclusion are removed directly from dirs in place using dirs.remove(d), which instructs os.walk not to traverse into those directory branches.

        # --- File processing (inline, sorted) ---
        for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(relpath):
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (.gitignore)]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (not in include list)]{C_RESET}")
                    continue

            # Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [size limit: {size_kb:.0f}KB]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                print(f"{C_GREEN}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [processed]{C_RESET}")
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: not a text file]{C_RESET}")
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: {e}]{C_RESET}")

Files within each retained directory are processed in deterministic alphabetical order (sorted(files)). The function resolves the appropriate path representation (relpath vs filepath) and evaluates the file against .gitignore rules, explicit glob exclusions (fnmatch), and inclusion constraints. If a file passes pattern checks, os.path.getsize checks against max_file_size. Files passing all filters are opened with encoding="utf-8-sig". If reading raises UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError, the file is flagged as non-text and omitted from files_dict.

    # --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    print("\n--- Crawl Summary ---")
    print(f"  Total found : {total_fetched}")
    print(f"{C_GREEN}  Processed   : {count_processed}{C_RESET}")
    if count_excluded > 0:
        print(f"{C_GRAY}  Excluded    : {count_excluded}{C_RESET}")
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Size limit  : {count_size_limit}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    if count_non_text > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Non-text    : {count_non_text}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    print("---------------------")

    return {"files": files_dict}

Once the directory walk completes, summary telemetry is aggregated and output to the terminal. The summary categorizes entries into total entries discovered, successfully processed text files, excluded files and directories, files exceeding byte size limits, and skipped non-text or unreadable files. The accumulated files_dict is then packaged into the output dictionary and returned.

Execution Example:

The following usage example is extracted directly from the module's executable entrypoint:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
    files_data = crawl_local_files(
        "..",
        exclude_patterns={
            "*.pyc",
            "__pycache__/*",
            ".venv/*",
            ".git/*",
            "docs/*",
            "output/*",
        },
    )
    print(f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
    for path in files_data["files"]:
        print(f"  {path}")

docs.title: In-Place Directory Pruning
docs.text: crawl_local_files uses Python's standard os.walk(directory) generator. To prevent walking down massive dependency trees (such as node_modules or .venv), the function mutates dirs in place using dirs.remove(d) after iterating over a snapshot copy (dirs.copy()). This prevents os.walk from descending into matching directory sub-trees, significantly reducing crawl latency and filesystem I/O.

docs.title: Path Normalization
docs.text: Directory patterns often contain trailing glob syntax such as docs/* or .git/*. The directory filtering logic applies pattern.removesuffix("/*") to normalize user-defined exclusion patterns prior to evaluating relative directory paths with fnmatch.fnmatch.

docs.title: BOM and Binary Detection
docs.text: All file read operations utilize utf-8-sig. This ensures that files generated on Windows systems containing UTF-8 Byte Order Marks (0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF) are loaded without corrupting the initial tokens of the content string. Binary files (such as compiled binaries, images, or archives) naturally fail UTF-8 decoding and trigger UnicodeDecodeError, allowing them to be classified as non-text without requiring external MIME-type inspection libraries.

It instructs the language model to analyze a provided index of file paths and return a strict YAML list containing only the integer indices corresponding to functional code modules (such as APIs, business logic, classes, and helper functions) while explicitly discarding UI layouts, project manifests, and static documentation.

Parameters: * project_name (str): The name or identifier of the project being documented. * file_listing (str): A pre-formatted, indexed list of candidate files within the repository.

def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:
    """Build the prompt for DeterministicFileMapper to filter non-code files.

    Used in api-reference mode to identify which files are actual code modules
    (APIs, functions, classes, business logic) vs. UI layouts, configs, assets.
    """
    return (
        f"For the project `{project_name}`, here is the list of all files in the codebase:\n\n"
        f"{file_listing}\n\n"
        f"Your task is to identify WHICH of these files are ACTUAL CODE files that contain "
        f"APIs, functions, classes, or core business logic.\n"
        f"EXCLUDE: UI layouts (like .xaml, .storyboard, .html), configuration files "
        f"(like .xml, .json, .manifest, .ini), static assets, build scripts "
        f"(like .csproj, .sln), and documentation.\n\n"
        f"Return ONLY a YAML list of the file indices that should be documented as code modules.\n\n"
        f"```yaml\n- 0\n- 1\n- 3\n```"
    )

The returned prompt specifies rigid negative constraints (e.g., excluding .xaml, .json, .csproj, and documentation files) to prevent the documentation pipeline from attempting to generate API reference chapters for non-executable or declarative files. By requesting output in a strict yaml ... code block containing integer indices, the downstream parser can reliably extract and map the valid file indices back to the source inventory.

Visibility: Public Signature: def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:

Description: Constructs a structured prompt instructing an LLM to generate a concise, multi-dimensional technical brief for an already generated chapter. The resulting brief acts as cross-chapter context in sequential pipeline executions, enabling subsequent chapter generation nodes to reference concepts, models, and boundaries established in previous chapters without exceeding context token limits.

The generated prompt enforces a 4-dimensional extraction model where each dimension is answered in 3 to 5 sentences: 1. Component scope and technical domain responsibilities. 2. Concrete classes, functions, interfaces, and service models. 3. Design patterns, architectural decisions, and error-handling strategies. 4. Inter-component boundaries, dependencies, and integration touchpoints.

Parameters: * chapter_num (int): The sequence index of the target chapter. * abstraction_name (str): The semantic title or abstraction name of the chapter component. * chapter_content (str): The full markdown text of the generated documentation chapter. * language (str, optional): The target output language. Defaults to "english". If a non-English string is provided, a localization instruction is prepended.

Returns: * str: The assembled prompt text including localization prefixes, the 4-part analytical rubric, and the chapter content payload.

Raises: * No explicit exceptions raised internally.

Example: 

def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:
    """Build the prompt for generating a technical summary of a written chapter.

    Used after each chapter is generated to create a concise technical summary
    for cross-chapter context. The summary is fed into subsequent chapters'
    prompts so the LLM maintains coherence across the full document.

    The summary captures 4 technical dimensions with 3-5 sentences each:
    1. Component scope & responsibility
    2. Key classes/services/functions and their roles
    3. Implementation patterns & architectural decisions
    4. Inter-component interfaces & dependencies
    """
    lang_instruction = f"Write the entire summary in {language.capitalize()}. " if language.lower() != "english" else ""
    return (
        f"{lang_instruction}"
        f"Summarize the following documentation chapter as a structured technical brief. "
        f"For EACH of the 4 points below, write 3-5 concise technical sentences:\n\n"
        f"(1) **Component Scope & Responsibility**: What is the main technical domain this "
        f"chapter covers? What problems does it solve and what role does it play in the system?\n\n"
        f"(2) **Key Technical Elements**: What are the specific classes, services, functions, "
        f"data models, or protocols discussed? Name them and describe their concrete roles.\n\n"
        f"(3) **Implementation Patterns & Architecture**: What design patterns, communication "
        f"protocols, data flow strategies, error handling mechanisms, or security measures "
        f"are covered? How are they implemented?\n\n"
        f"(4) **System Integration & Dependencies**: How does this component interface with "
        f"other parts of the system? What does it consume from or provide to other components? "
        f"What are the key integration points?\n\n"
        f"---\n"
        f"Chapter {chapter_num}: {abstraction_name}\n"
        f"{chapter_content}"
    )

The function handles dynamic localization by conditionally prefixing the prompt with Write the entire summary in {language.capitalize()}. when language is not set to "english". The structured 4-part rubric prevents vague summaries by forcing concrete naming of classes, services, and integration points, ensuring downstream LLM calls in nodes receive high-density technical context.

Visibility: Public Signature: def build_mkdocs_config(site_name: str, nav_yaml: str) -> str:

Description: Formats and returns a complete mkdocs.yml configuration string. It configures the MkDocs Material theme, clipboard copy buttons, search plugins, inline syntax highlighting, and custom Mermaid fence handlers (pymdownx.superfences configured with fence_code_format).

The function splits the supplied nav_yaml input string to strip any leading nav: header line and embeds the remaining hierarchy under a root - Home: index.md navigation entry.

Parameters: * site_name (str): The documentation site title displayed in the header and navigation bar. * nav_yaml (str): A YAML-formatted navigation hierarchy string generated during documentation compilation.

Returns: * str: The serialized YAML configuration file content ready to be written to mkdocs.yml.

def build_mkdocs_config(site_name: str, nav_yaml: str) -> str:
    """Build a complete mkdocs.yml for local --mkdocs output.

    Generates a ready-to-use MkDocs Material config with:
    - Material theme with code copy buttons
    - Syntax highlighting (pymdownx.highlight + inlinehilite)
    - Mermaid diagram rendering via pymdownx.superfences custom fences
    - Navigation from the generated nav_snippet

    Users can run `mkdocs serve` or `mkdocs build` directly in the output dir.
    """
    # Extract nav items from nav_snippet (strip the "nav:" header line)
    nav_lines = nav_yaml.split("\n")
    nav_body = "\n".join(nav_lines[1:]) if nav_lines else ""

    return (
        f"site_name: '{site_name}'\n"
        f"theme:\n"
        f"  name: material\n"
        f"  features:\n"
        f"    - content.code.copy\n"
        f"plugins:\n"
        f"  - search\n"
        f"  - panzoom\n"
        f"markdown_extensions:\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.highlight:\n"
        f"      anchor_linenums: true\n"
        f"      use_pygments: true\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.superfences:\n"
        f"      custom_fences:\n"
        f"        - name: mermaid\n"
        f"          class: mermaid\n"
        f"          format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.inlinehilite\n"
        f"nav:\n"
        f"  - Home: index.md\n"
        f"{nav_body}\n"
    )

The navigation normalization logic inspects nav_yaml line-by-line using split("\n"). By taking nav_lines[1:], it safely discards redundant top-level nav: tags emitted by language models or navigation builders, splicing the clean YAML child tree directly below the default root page (- Home: index.md). The returned YAML string allows users to immediately run mkdocs serve or mkdocs build on the generated output directory.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The utils.token_utils module provides specialized utility functions and global state caching for calculating, estimating, and logging prompt token metrics across pipeline execution stages. Managing token counts is critical in large language model (LLM) orchestration pipelines to prevent context-window truncation, optimize payload allocation, and generate diagnostic telemetry for downstream performance analysis.

This module encapsulates token-counting logic using the tiktoken library with a lazy-loaded singleton pattern targeting the cl100k_base encoding (standard for OpenAI models such as GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo). To ensure runtime resilience in environments where tokenizer vocabulary binaries or native dependencies are missing or fail to initialize, it implements a character-based heuristic fallback (len(text) // 4). In addition, the module provides visual terminal telemetry using ANSI escape codes alongside structured single-line output to the shared application logger (llm_logger).

docs.title: _get_encoding()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Internal Helper) Signature: def _get_encoding() -> tiktoken.Encoding | None:

Description: Lazily resolves and caches the tiktoken encoding instance for cl100k_base. If the encoding has not yet been initialized, it attempts to load it from tiktoken. Any encountered exception (e.g., missing tokenizer cache, network timeout during vocabulary download, or environment constraints) is caught, leaving _encoding as None to enable graceful fallback without raising unhandled exceptions.

Parameters: * None.

Returns: * tiktoken.Encoding | None: The loaded cl100k_base encoding instance if successful; otherwise, None.

Raises: * No exceptions are propagated; all initialization errors are caught internally.

Core Implementation: 

def _get_encoding():
    global _encoding
    if _encoding is None:
        try:
            _encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
        except Exception:
            _encoding = None
    return _encoding

The function relies on the global _encoding reference to maintain a singleton pattern across the lifetime of the process. If initialization fails on the first invocation, subsequent calls will attempt resolution again unless _encoding was set to a valid object. Once resolved, subsequent invocations return the cached object immediately, minimizing runtime overhead during repeated token calculations.

docs.title: count_tokens()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:

Description: Calculates the exact or approximate token count for a given text string. If the string is empty or evaluates to falsy, it immediately returns 0. When an encoding object is available from _get_encoding(), the function encodes the text using disallowed_special=() (which disables special token parsing errors and treats all special tokens as literal strings) and returns the length of the resulting token array. If the tokenizer is unavailable, it falls back to estimating tokens using the standard 4-character-per-token heuristic (len(text) // 4).

Parameters: * text (str): The raw text or prompt content whose tokens are to be counted.

Returns: * int: Total number of tokens computed via tiktoken encoding or estimated via character heuristics.

Raises: * No exceptions are explicitly raised.

Example: 

def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Count tokens using tiktoken, with fallback to chars/4."""
    if not text:
        return 0
    enc = _get_encoding()
    if enc:
        return len(enc.encode(text, disallowed_special=()))
    return len(text) // 4

This method is the primary token-counting interface for prompt construction and payload boundary validation across workflow nodes. By passing disallowed_special=(), the tokenizer does not raise ValueError when encountering control tokens (such as <|endoftext|>), ensuring safe execution on arbitrary source code content.

docs.title: log_token_estimation()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def log_token_estimation(node_name: str, prompt_content: str, max_tokens: int, token_usage: dict | None = None) -> None:

Description: Computes token volume for a prompt payload, calculates its percentage relative to the node's maximum capacity limit, and formats detailed diagnostics for terminal display and structured file logging. If an optional breakdown dictionary (token_usage) is provided, it calculates individual proportional percentages, pads labels for visual alignment, and includes the breakdown in both stdout and log records.

Parameters: * node_name (str): Identifier or human-readable label of the pipeline node currently executing (e.g., "GenerateOverviewNode"). * prompt_content (str): The complete prompt payload text passed to the LLM. * max_tokens (int): Maximum context token threshold allowed for the node. * token_usage (dict | None, optional): Key-value mapping representing sub-component token contributions (e.g., {"System Prompt": 500, "Context Files": 12000}). Defaults to None.

Returns: * None

Raises: * No exceptions are raised.

Example: 

def log_token_estimation(node_name: str, prompt_content: str, max_tokens: int, token_usage: dict | None = None) -> None:
    token_count = count_tokens(prompt_content)
    percentage = (token_count / max_tokens) * 100 if max_tokens else 0

    # Build token usage string if provided
    usage_str = ""
    usage_log_str = ""
    if token_usage:
        # Find the longest label for alignment
        max_label_len = max(len(label) for label in token_usage)
        lines = []
        log_parts = []
        for label, value in token_usage.items():
            pct = (value / token_count * 100) if token_count else 0
            padded_label = label.ljust(max_label_len)
            lines.append(f"\t{padded_label} : {value:,} ({pct:.0f}%)")
            log_parts.append(f"{label}={value:,} ({pct:.0f}%)")
        usage_str = "\n" + "\n".join(lines)
        usage_log_str = " | " + " | ".join(log_parts)

    # Console output (yellow) with token usage on separate lines
    print(f"\033[93m[Token Analytics] {node_name}: {token_count:,} / {max_tokens:,} tokens ({percentage:.1f}% capacity){usage_str}\033[0m")

    # File log stays single-line for parseability
    logger.info(f"NODE EXEC | node={node_name} | prompt_tokens={token_count:,} / {max_tokens:,} ({percentage:.1f}% capacity){usage_log_str}")

log_token_estimation writes human-readable, multi-line ANSI yellow output to standard output (sys.stdout) while concurrently emitting a compact, single-line log message to logger.info(). The single-line log format ensures downstream log ingestion pipelines and log parsers can ingest execution metrics without handling multiline log entry fragmentation.
